newsitem.title: UK: Lufthansa Cargo has until 98 to make money.
newsitem.headline: Lufthansa Cargo has until 98 to make money.

text.p: Lufthansa Cargo AG has been told by its main board to become profitable by 1998 at the latest, or otherwise cease to exist as an autonomous unit, said its senior vice-president Europe and Africa Joachim Haas.
Speaking at an air cargo industry conference here, he said that ideally parent company Deutsche Lufthansa AG wanted its LCAG airfreight division to show a profit for 1997.
"But if profitability is not achieved by 1998, then LCAG will be no more -- it will be re-integrated as part of the passenger division," he told delegates.
LCAG reported a profit of 20 million marks for 1995. Haas said it made a loss last year but he declined to comment on the amount as figures had yet to be finalised.
During 1997, he said, LCAG would invest 40 million marks on "redesigning our internal processes".
This, he added, would include investment in barcoding -- "each and every piece of our cargo will have a barcode on it by August 15" -- weighing and messaging technology.
Haas told Reuters that to survive, LCAG would in future have to become more market -- rather than operations -- orientated, but he declined to elaborate.
Haas would not comment on the possibility of LCAG outsourcing the ground handling side of its business.

He told the conference that the way to achieve better yields was for airlines and airfreight forwarders to work closely together in their dealings with shippers and consignees, rather than persist with airline-forwarder and forwarder-shipper trading practices.
This, he said, was directly opposite to the approach being adopted by KLM Royal Dutch Airlines, which has recently been focusing attention on direct dealing with shippers.
"My experience is that apart from only a few of them, most shippers wanting to use airlines directly (omitting a middle-man forwarder), do so to try and push rates down," he stated.
"We have asked forwarders for the names of their top shippers," said Haas, noting that most forwarders had complied with this request despite initial reluctance.
"Better communication with shippers does not mean us selling against forwarders," he stressed.
He said that LCAG and its forwarders had together talked with about 50 top shippers in continental Europe.
This joint approach, he added, had helped shift the focus of discussions from just rate levels to how to improve service standards.
As a result, he said he had seen service levels and yields rising.
Haas added he hoped the same approach could be adopted in Britain.
He said he had been told by LCAG in London that this joint airline/forwarder relationship and approach to shippers would be impossible to implement in the UK.
"I know that it is a forwarder-dominated market in the UK, but we do not have to accept that," he said.
